analysis.headline: With zero cosponsors and no committee action after two Senate floor remarks, Sen. Leahy's windfall oil profits tax died in the Senate Finance Committee at the end of the 106th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: During the fall 2000 heating-oil price spike, this bill would have imposed a 100% excise tax on any oil-industry profit the Federal Trade Commission judged to be above a "reasonable" level, going back to January 1, 2000. The money would have gone into a new trust fund paying for heating assistance for households (75%) and small businesses (25%). It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never acted on before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and small businesses facing record heating-oil prices that winter would have received heating assistance funded entirely by a tax on oil companies' profits above what the FTC deemed reasonable.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households and small businesses facing high heating bills

how_it_helps.text: The bill cites Energy Department estimates that heating-oil inventories were 36% below the prior year nationwide and 65% below in New England, with prices expected to hit an all-time high in the winter of 2000-2001, and directs the new fund's money to heating assistance for consumers and small businesses.
Up to 75% of the tax revenue would fund heating assistance for consumers and up to 25% for small businesses, via a new Windfall Oil Profits Trust Fund. [S3]

The bill's stated purpose is to "transfer windfall profits from the oil industry" to fund that heating assistance, noting that 14 major petroleum companies' combined net income more than doubled in the second quarter of 2000 to $10.3 billion.

analysis.who_pays: Oil producers would pay a 100% tax on profits above an FTC-determined reasonable level, retroactive to January 1, 2000. If producers passed costs through to prices, consumers could pay more at the pump, partially offsetting the assistance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Major oil and petroleum product producers

drawbacks.text: The tax applies retroactively to crude oil and petroleum products removed on or after January 1, 2000, meaning it would tax profits companies had already earned under the old rules. [S3]

The FTC — an antitrust agency, not a tax authority — would be handed the open-ended job of deciding what a "reasonable" profit is for every removal of crude oil or petroleum fuel, which critics would call arbitrary and unworkable. [S3]

An honest supporter would acknowledge that a 100% tax on producer profits could be passed through into higher gasoline and heating-oil prices, raising costs for the same consumers the bill aims to help, and that using the tax code to claw back profits may discourage production during a supply squeeze.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The help is real and targeted — heating aid during an acute price spike, paid for by the industry booking record profits. But the design is aggressive: a retroactive 100% tax keyed to a regulator's judgment of "reasonable" profit, with real risk that costs pass through to the same consumers it aims to help. It was a message bill as much as a workable one.

outcome.mechanism: Leahy introduced it with no cosponsors, spoke about it twice on the Senate floor, and it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the Congress ended on January 3, 2001, without a hearing, a vote, or any other action.

narrative.text: Sen. Leahy introduced the bill on September 27, 2000, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance. [S5]
Leahy delivered introductory remarks on the bill again on October 25, 2000, but the Finance Committee took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress. [S5]

The bill's findings documented that major oil companies' quarterly profits roughly doubled year-over-year in 2000 — for example Exxon Mobil's $4.53 billion in the second quarter of 2000, up 123% — while gasoline hit a national average record of $1.68 per gallon and heating-oil inventories ran far below prior-year levels. [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The oil companies kept their record 2000 profits untouched, and no heating assistance was funded from their excess earnings; low-income households facing record winter heating-oil prices got nothing from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major oil companies kept record profits

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor twice (September 27 and October 25, 2000), and referred it to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — after it was referred on September 27, 2000.

against.name: Sen. William Roth
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration before the Congress ended.

against.name: Petroleum industry
against.role: Major oil producers and refiners targeted by the tax
against.what_they_did: The bill would have taxed 100% of their profits above an FTC-determined reasonable level, retroactively to January 1, 2000; no publicly recorded campaign over this particular bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and the Republican-led Finance Committee never acted on it, so there was no recorded bipartisan or floor vote to measure.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed a 100% excise tax on all profits the FTC judged above reasonable, retroactive to January 1, 2000, clawing back a large share of the record profits documented in its findings. Its defeat left those profits intact; any pass-through of the tax into consumer fuel prices would have put the industry's interest directly against the households the bill tried to help.

industries.industry: Low-income home heating assistance providers (LIHEAP-type programs and fuel dealers serving assisted households)
industries.note: The bill would have created a dedicated funding stream (75% consumer / 25% small business) for heating assistance during a winter of record expected heating-oil prices and sharply depleted inventories. With the bill's death, that funding never existed.
